idiom_name: published contract + plugin descriptor + registry + dynamic loader + lifecycle
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: publish a narrow contract (interfaces plus the host services a plugin may use) in a unit both sides depend on, and let every plugin declare its identity, version, required contract version and the extension points it fills in a descriptor the host can read without executing plugin code. Keep a registry that maps extension point -> plugin id -> factory, load the code through the runtime's dynamic loader, validate descriptor and contract version before instantiating, hand the plugin only the published host services, then run it through an explicit lifecycle (register, activate, deactivate, unload) with unload in reverse dependency order. Isolate plugin code to the level its trustworthiness deserves, and keep the core free of plugin-specific logic.
code_sketch:
contract: extension_points.Formatter = { format(doc) -> bytes }
# plugin descriptor, readable without loading code:
# plugins/csv/plugin.json
# { "id": "csv", "contract_version": 2, "provides": ["formatter"], "entry": "csv:Formatter" }
reg = Registry.scan("plugins/*/plugin.json", contract_version=2)
reg.validate()          # fail closed on mismatch or missing capability
reg.activate_all()      # descriptors -> loader -> factory -> host services
# later
reg.unload_all()        # reverse dependency order
pitfalls: Reading a descriptor by executing plugin code: discovery must not run plugin code, or one broken plugin takes the whole host down at start-up.
Skipping contract/version validation at the boundary, so an incompatible plugin fails later at an unrelated call site instead of at load time.
Shipping without a lifecycle and an unload path: registrations, threads, handles and cache entries leak back into the host on every reload.

Wrong move: expose broad mutable host internals to extensions -> one plugin can violate core invariants and make failures order-dependent -> instead publish narrow capability interfaces and reject undeclared access at the boundary.

Wrong move: treat a plugin protocol as an unversioned in-process ABI -> upgrades fail at load time or corrupt the host -> instead negotiate an explicit contract version and use an isolation boundary when compatibility or trust requires it.

Wrong move: import every plugin eagerly during discovery -> one broken extension delays startup and wastes memory -> instead parse manifests without execution and activate lazily with failure containment.
